Prepare survey data for cluster analysis

Source: R/seg_prep.R
seg_prep_data.Rd

Prepares a (haven-labelled) data frame for segmentation: selects the clustering variables, handles missing values, rescales the variables and (optionally) computes a distance matrix using factoextra::get_dist() or cluster::daisy().

Usage

seg_prep_data(
  data,
  vars = dplyr::everything(),
  id = NULL,
  missing = c("omit", "mean", "median", "mice", "none"),
  max_missing_prop = NULL,
  scale = c("z", "range", "none"),
  distance = "euclidean",
  distance_engine = c("auto", "get_dist", "daisy"),
  compute_distance = TRUE,
  imputation_args = list(),
  daisy_args = list(),
  seed = 123,
  verbose = TRUE
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, typically a haven-labelled tibble (e.g. read in with haven::read_sav(path, user_na = TRUE)). User-defined missing values (e.g. 99 = "don't know") must already be recoded to NA, e.g. with dp_recode_missing().

vars

<tidy-select> Clustering variables. Must be numeric (haven-labelled numeric variables are fine). Defaults to all variables.

id

Optional single string naming an identifier column in data. Its values are used as row names of the prepared data and labels of the distance matrix (e.g. for factoextra::fviz_dist()).

missing

How to handle missing values in the clustering variables. Respondents without any valid answer on the clustering variables are always removed first.

  • "omit" (default): listwise deletion of respondents with any missing value.

  • "mean" / "median": replace missing values with the variable mean / median.

  • "mice": single imputation with mice::mice() (predictive mean matching by default, see imputation_args). Preserves the relationships between variables better than mean/median imputation.

  • "none": keep missing values. Only allowed with distance_engine = "daisy", which computes dissimilarities from the available pairs of values.

max_missing_prop

Optional number between 0 and 1. Respondents with a higher proportion of missing values across the clustering variables are removed before missing is applied. Useful to combine with imputation, e.g. max_missing_prop = 0.2, missing = "mice". NULL (default) keeps all respondents.

scale

How to rescale the clustering variables:

  • "z" (default): z-standardization (mean 0, SD 1), see base::scale().

  • "range": min-max scaling to the range 0 to 1.

  • "none": keep the original values, e.g. if all variables share the same response scale and differences in variance are meaningful.

distance

Distance measure. With distance_engine = "get_dist" one of "euclidean", "maximum", "manhattan", "canberra", "binary", "minkowski", "pearson", "spearman" or "kendall". With distance_engine = "daisy" one of "euclidean", "manhattan" or "gower". Defaults to "euclidean".

distance_engine

Which function computes the distance matrix: "auto" (default) uses cluster::daisy() for distance = "gower" and factoextra::get_dist() otherwise; "get_dist" or "daisy" force the respective function.

compute_distance

Logical. Whether to compute the distance matrix. Defaults to TRUE. Set to FALSE for large samples if only the prepared data is needed (e.g. for k-means), as the distance matrix grows with the square of the number of respondents.

imputation_args

A list of arguments passed to mice::mice() when missing = "mice", added to the defaults method = "pmm" (predictive mean matching) and printFlag = FALSE, e.g. list(method = "cart"). Only a single imputation (m = 1) is used. A seed given here takes precedence over seed.

daisy_args

A list of further arguments passed to cluster::daisy(), e.g. list(type = list(ordratio = c("F50_0_1", "F50_0_2"))) to treat variables as ordinal when using Gower distance.

seed

Random seed for the imputation with missing = "mice", which makes the imputed values reproducible. The global random seed is left untouched. Defaults to 123. NULL uses the current random state (not reproducible).

verbose

Logical. Whether to print a summary of the preparation steps. Defaults to TRUE.

Value

An object of class seg_prep, a list with the elements:

  • data: tibble with the prepared (cleaned, imputed, rescaled) clustering variables, keeping their variable labels. Use this as input for clustering algorithms such as k-means.

  • data_full: the original data (all columns, labels intact) restricted to the respondents retained in data, in the same order. Use this to profile the resulting segments.

  • dist: the distance matrix (class dist), or NULL if compute_distance = FALSE.

  • row_index: integer positions of the retained respondents in data.

  • settings: list of the settings used, including the parameters needed to prepare new respondents in the same way (see predict.seg_cluster()): scaling (tibble with the center and scale of each clustering variable), impute_values (the means or medians used for imputation), imputation_args and seed.

  • info: list with the number of respondents before and after the preparation, the number of imputed values and dropped constant variables.

Details

Cluster analysis groups respondents that are similar. How similarity is measured is defined by the distance measure, which is therefore one of the most important choices of a segmentation. The descriptions below follow datanovia. \(x\) and \(y\) denote the answers of two respondents on the \(n\) clustering variables.

Distance-based measures

These measures compare the values of two respondents: respondents with similar answers on all variables are close.

  • Euclidean ("euclidean", default): \(d(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2}\). The straight-line distance. Large differences weigh more, as they are squared. Use it as the default, in particular with k-means and Ward's hierarchical clustering, which are built on it (k-means always uses Euclidean distances, whatever is specified here).

  • Manhattan ("manhattan"): \(d(x, y) = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i - y_i|\). The sum of the absolute differences ("city block" distance). Less sensitive to outliers and single extreme answers than Euclidean. Use it for rating scales, where differences of one scale point simply add up, or if the data contains outliers; works well with PAM.

  • Maximum ("maximum", Chebyshev distance): \(d(x, y) = \max_i |x_i - y_i|\). Only the largest difference on any single variable counts. Rarely useful for survey data, as a single item dominates the distance.

  • Minkowski ("minkowski"): \(d(x, y) = (\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i - y_i|^p)^{1/p}\), a generalization of Manhattan (\(p = 1\)) and Euclidean (\(p = 2\), used here).

  • Canberra ("canberra"): \(d(x, y) = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i - y_i| / (|x_i| + |y_i|)\). A weighted Manhattan distance, in which differences between small values weigh more. Use it only for non-negative data (e.g. counts or shares, with scale = "range" or "none"), not with z-standardized data.

  • Binary ("binary"): the proportion of variables in which only one of the two respondents has a non-zero value, among the variables in which at least one has a non-zero value. Use it for 0/1 data, e.g. multiple-response questions (with scale = "none").

Correlation-based measures

These measures compare the profiles of two respondents across the variables: two respondents are close if their answers go up and down together, regardless of their overall level. The distance is \(d(x, y) = 1 - r(x, y)\), where \(r\) is a correlation coefficient between the answers of the two respondents (range 0 to 2).

  • Pearson ("pearson"): based on the Pearson correlation.

  • Spearman ("spearman"): based on the rank correlation. More robust to outliers and only assumes a monotonic relation; well suited for ordinal rating scales.

  • Kendall ("kendall"): based on the proportion of concordant pairs of ranks. Similar to Spearman, more robust with many ties, but slower.

Use them when the pattern of answers matters more than their level, e.g. to reduce the influence of response styles: a respondent who agrees a bit more with every item (acquiescence) has the same profile as a respondent with the same relative preferences. They require a fair number of clustering variables, as the correlation is computed across them for each pair of respondents.

Gower distance

Gower ("gower", via cluster::daisy()): each variable contributes a distance between 0 and 1 (the absolute difference divided by the range for numeric variables, 0/1 for a mismatch for nominal variables, ranks for ordinal variables), and the distance is the average over all variables that both respondents answered. Use it for mixed data types (see daisy_args) or to keep missing values (missing = "none"). Combine it with PAM or hierarchical clustering, not with k-means.

Choosing a distance measure and scaling

  • Typical attitude batteries on the same rating scale: Euclidean (default) or Manhattan; Spearman or Pearson to cluster on answer patterns.

  • Data with outliers or extreme answers: Manhattan (with PAM).

  • Binary data: binary; mixed data types or missing values: Gower.

Distance-based measures depend on the scale of the variables: variables with a large range or variance dominate the distance. Variables measured on different scales must therefore be rescaled (scale = "z" or "range"). For items on the same scale, z-standardization gives each item the same weight; use scale = "none" if differences in variance are meaningful.

See also

seg_distance() to compute a distance matrix on already prepared data.

Examples

# \donttest{
prep <- seg_prep_data(
  sm_synthetic,
  vars = dplyr::starts_with("F50_0_"),
  id = "id",
  missing = "mice",
  max_missing_prop = 0.2
)
#> 
#> ── Data prepared for cluster analysis ──
#> 
#> • Clustering variables: 20
#> • Respondents: 1401 in, 1371 retained
#> • Without any valid answer: 1 respondent removed
#> • Missing threshold: 29 respondent(s) with more than 20% missing removed
#> • Missing values: "mice" (0 respondents removed, 407 values imputed)
#> • Scaling: "z"
#> • Distance: euclidean (get_dist)
# }
